html:
A stone tablet set up in 781 in Chang'an, capital of Tang China, that tells the story of the Church of the East there over its first 150 years. It is the main evidence for Christians in Tang China.

The Church of the East, often called Nestorian, was based in Persia and spread east along the Silk Road. The stele says a monk named Aluoben reached Chang'an in 635 and that Emperor Taizong let him translate scriptures and build a church. The Chinese called the faith Jingjiao, the "luminous teaching". The text, in Chinese with Syriac names and notes, explains Christian belief using Buddhist and Daoist words.

In 845 the emperor Wuzong turned on foreign religions, above all Buddhism, and the church in China faded. The stele was buried and only dug up again in the 1620s. Jesuit missionaries, successors of Matteo Ricci, hailed it as proof of an ancient Chinese Christianity. It now stands in the Forest of Steles museum in Xi'an.
sum: A stone tablet set up in 781 in Chang'an, capital of Tang China, that tells the story of the Church of the East there over its first 150 years. It is the main evidence for Christians in Tang China.
